articles.title: Ex-Google engineer says he believes right now it looks like humans don’t have more than 10 years on the clock
articles.summary: A former Google AI expert is so convinced that artificial intelligence (AI) will wipe out humanity that he stopped putting money into his retirement fund
articles.body: A former Google AI expert is so convinced that artificial intelligence (AI) will wipe out humanity that he stopped putting money into his retirement fund a decade ago. Machine learning researcher Nate Soares, who previously worked as a software engineer at both Google and Microsoft, recently shared the grim outlook during a recent podcast interview with The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson. According to Soares, there is a greater than 50% chance that AI will cause human extinction within the next 10 years.“I do not save for retirement now. I have a 401K from when I worked at Google, but I haven’t contributed to it for like a decade,” Soares said on the podcast. His comments came about two months after three researchers with the industry giant Anthropic claimed that AI could kill off humanity within the decade. Jacob Coxon resigned from his job in protest claiming Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat.Living under the shadow of extinctionDespite his bleak forecast, Soares said he does not believe human extinction is inevitable, and he spends his time doing everything he can to prevent it. Soares now serves as president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, a Berkeley-based nonprofit known for “AI doomerism”. He compared the daily reality of worrying about AI to how people have historically coped with the threat of nuclear annihilation.“It’s maybe the first time that we lived under the shadow of every human dying at once, but personally, we’ve always lived under the shadow of plague, shadow of war. And what you do is you do what you can and then you live a good life,” Soares said.Why current AI flaws do not reassure former Google, Microsoft engineerDuring the interview, Thompson pushed back on the doomsday scenario, pointing out that even the most advanced AI systems today still run into plenty of bumps and limitations. Soares brushed off that reassurance, comparing the current state of AI to the early days of the automobile.“You could imagine a lot of horses looking at the development of the car and saying, 'Well, there’s all these things the car can’t do yet’. We are seeing AIs get better and better at things. We’re seeing them able to take on longer and longer tasks,” Soares told Thompson, as per New York Post.When it comes to the economy, Soares also made it clear he isn't worried about mass unemployment.“I’m not an 'AI jobs apocalypse guy’. I’m an 'AI kills all humans' guy, in which case you’ll be at full employment actually. We’ll be at full employment the moment before we’re all killed off,” he said.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
articles.summary: Large language models can now redesign your TV and upgrade your camera for you. Is the physical world ready to be Claude Code-d?﻿
articles.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of. For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?” Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen. Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. Even when they don’t, odds are good that there’s another way in. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking. Again, few of the technical capabilities here are new, and enterprising developers have been doing this kind of work for many years. Some have even been using AI for several years to make the work easier. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. And over the course of 2026, more and more people began pointing that capability at their hardware. How it’s going Now, it seems, all hardware is hacker hardware. Camera enthusiasts embraced the possibilities of vibe hacking as fast as anyone, using LLMs to repackage their camera software in all sorts of ways. Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like everyone is using AI to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware. The music world is being similarly upended. Budding musicians are turning cheap synths into powerful new kinds of gear, and a cheap gadget known as the M-Vave FM-1 has become a popular target for custom firmware and new features. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. The FM-1 is cheap, it’s easy to hack, and it’s raising questions about what higher-end manufacturers can even do to compete. Gamers, who are also using AI to decompile and mod the games they love, are using LLMs to add new features to their consoles. One vibe coder found a way to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have built scripts that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices. In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Game makers are looking for ways to protect their work from being decompiled and made available for free and on other platforms. Luke Dicken, a longtime gaming executive who was recently Take-Two’s head of artificial intelligence, recently predicted to Kotaku that the industry will start to embrace “more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.” Hardware makers will push harder to lock down their systems; companies across the board will pursue legal action to protect their intellectual property. All this hardware access also creates new risks for users. When you install a vibe-coded version of your camera’s firmware, you are now well outside the bounds of what the camera manufacturer is equipped to help you solve. You might be stuck asking Claude to fix the problems Claude created. As Ritchie Roesch wrote recently at Fuji X Weekly, “It’s not so much if someone’s camera will become a permanent paperweight, it’s a matter of when and how many, and whether it will be yours.” The safer (and less litigious) route for the enterprising vibe hacker lies in an entirely new kind of hardware. ESP32 modules, which package networking chips, microphones, speakers, and more into a simple and hacker-friendly package, are suddenly everywhere in hardware communities. (Think Raspberry Pis, but even cheaper and more versatile.) So sure, you can use Claude Code to jailbreak and de-Amazon your Kindle, but why do that when you can buy a device like the M5Stack PaperMono, an ESP32-based e-paper device you can make into whatever you want? ESP32 modules are perfectly suited to help you build the kind of hyper-specific device Apple or Samsung would never consider. With a few dollars and a few prompts, you can build a way to see real-time sea conditions, rig up a monitor for your whole DJ system, or just play Metal Gear Solid on the go. You can even have a dedicated device for your family’s shopping list. What happens next The arms race between device manufacturers and vibe hackers is only going to continue. As AI models get more powerful, and both the tools and their users get more sophisticated, it’ll be easier and easier for anyone to point their bot at their TV, their car, or their washing machine and see what happens. Some manufacturers will try their best to keep the hackers out; others will look for ways to safely embrace them. Some users will find incredible new functionality for their tech; others will find they’ve created extraordinarily large and expensive paperweights. Before long, we’re going to see a lot of ESP32 devices turned into more consumer-friendly hardware. Meta is already leading the charge with its Muse Charm and the Muse Gadgets program, through which you can either buy a nicely packaged ESP32 module or use your own to quickly spin up a dedicated AI device. This kind of gadget — just a simple computing module in a pretty box — is going to be everywhere. At the same time, we’re already seeing some vibe hackers turn into proper software vendors. Gathin, for instance, has spent a lot of time reckoning with the responsibility he feels for what happens when people use CleanYourTV to hack their televisions. He’s tweaked the prompts he shares to first take a backup of your TV’s software in order to make it easy to restore if something goes wrong, and to make note of every change it makes along the way. The CleanYourTV system also checks its progress as it goes and spins up agents to manually test if something has gone wrong, and Gathin hopes it’s increasingly foolproof. But it’s not foolproof. It might never be. Devices change all the time; every software update introduces new possibilities and new problems. So Gathin recommends the same thing I hear from vibe coders and vibe hackers all the time: Never give the bots access to something you can’t afford to lose. “Even for fiddling with stuff,” he says, “I have an external computer which runs through Linux. So I just use it like a sandbox environment to test things out.” If you’re going to try and vibe-hack your phone (which lots of people are doing) or your computer (which lots of people are also doing), do it carefully. And make lots of backups. By the way * If you are vibe-hacking an existing gadget, you are practically always voiding your warranty. There are no guarantees, and you definitely can’t count on customer support to get you out of a jam or offer you a refund. * You can buy ESP32 devices from lots of places, but a lot of folks recommend starting on Waveshare, which has a big selection and pretty good prices. * Espressif, which created the ESP chip, also recently launched its own development system, called ESP-Claw. It’s designed to make programming your ESP device even simpler. * Raspberry Pis are also good vibe-hacking devices! You can even run Claude Code on a Raspberry Pi… to hack a Raspberry Pi. Read this * Check out Terrence O’Brien’s deeper look at the AI vibe-hacking world, and the ways in which these new synths — in particular the FM-1 — are changing the way people think about music gear. * Elektor has a good piece about the history and technical details of ESP32, which goes back more than a decade. * Richie at Fuji X Weekly posted a follow-up to that original blog about vibe-coded firmware, diving into both the debate about AI in general and about what it even means to use a particular camera. “If that camera can be hacked with AI vibe coded 3rd party firmware to change its functions and features, is it still the same camera?” * Just as AI is being used to revive and improve old gadgets, The Verge’s Andrew Webster found that so too are old games being reimagined with AI. For better and for worse. * I wrote a while back about the personal software revolution and how vibe coding meant everyone could build the exact software they want. The same thing is coming fast to hardware everywhere.

articles.title: RAF's next fighter jet could be last crewed combat aircraft
articles.summary: The head of the RAF said AI-enabled and uncrewed aircrafts are expected to start flying in UK airspace next year.
articles.body:
Britain's next-generation fighter jet could be the last crewed combat aircraft the UK builds, the head of the RAF has said.

Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, said Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled, uncrewed aircraft would "transform military aviation".

His comments refer to the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), a partnership between the UK, Italy and Japan to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet, expected to enter service by 2035.

The aircraft, commonly known as Tempest , is expected to provide speed stealth, use advanced sensors and even AI to assist the human pilot when they are overwhelmed, or under extreme stress.

Writing in the Telegraph , Sir Harv said the GCAP aircraft was "perhaps the last crewed fighter we will ever build", not because people would become less important, but because advances in technology were changing the nature of air combat.

He said AI and machines would take on "the most dangerous tasks instead of humans", while stressing that technology should enhance human judgement and "not replace accountability". He added: "Uncrewed fighter jets will start flying in UK airspace next year. This is exciting and necessary in equal measure."

Sir Harv also said the RAF of the future would combine Typhoons and F-35s with autonomous systems.

The programme was announced in 2022 by the UK, Italy and Japan, which are jointly developing the aircraft. In July, the three countries signed a £4.6bn contract covering the next phase of its design through industry joint venture Edgewing.

According to GCAP, the aircraft will be powered by advanced data processing and artificial intelligence, while also featuring enhanced stealth technology. The UK government says the project already supports 3,500 jobs and 1,000 apprenticeships.

Canada was granted "observer nation" status in July, giving it privileged access to the programme without a decision-making role.

In October, Prime Minister, Andy Burnham , said the UK government would "seek to progress" Germany joining GCAP. He said the partnership could also support cooperation on issues including "countering hybrid attacks" and "countering interference in our democratic processes".

articles.title: Elon Musk warns data center delays could leave AI companies short on cash: 'Going to be nuts'
articles.summary: Elon Musk's warning of a "cash shortage" comes on the heels of an intense market sell-off in AI and tech.
articles.body:
Elon Musk warned that the AI buildout may face serious headwinds come next year.

The SpaceX CEO predicted a "cash shortage" for AI companies.

His statement comes on the heels of an intense market sell-off in AI and tech.

Elon Musk said AI companies may soon run into serious cash shortages as they wait for revenue-generating data centers to come online.

The SpaceX and Tesla CEO replied to an X post on Saturday that showed comparatively low stock valuations for semiconductor manufacturers, relative to their expected profits.

This could suggest that investors are bearish on AI-powering chip companies continuing to notch soaring profits in the race for compute — a sign that data center construction may face serious headwinds in the near future.

"The cash shortage is also going to be nuts next year," Musk said, adding that delays in data center activations would require "hundreds of billions" in more capital for AI companies.

Tech stocks in US markets took it on the chin last week. The S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory on Friday, meaning they had fallen at least 10% from recent highs.

The market carnage prompted some to speculate that the AI bubble had popped.

Financial regulators in semiconductor-heavy Taiwan on Saturday said they would limit short selling — an action similar to one taken by US regulators during the 2008 housing crisis.

Though leading AI and AI-adjacent companies like Meta, Microsoft, and Anthropic are reporting growing revenue, they're also spending massive sums to secure compute — powered by key hardware that enables chatbots and other AI tools.

Compute is largely provided by data centers, which have faced their own series of setbacks recently, from backlash from the communities where they are being built to the blue midterm wave and construction delays.

And without a reliable network of data centers, AI companies are hobbled in their ability to scale to meet investor demand. Data center operators, meanwhile, are left at the altar with their multibillion-dollar investments failing to generate revenue.

"Getting this amount of compute turned on, cooled and working reliably is incredibly hard," Musk said.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

articles.title: Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash
articles.summary: Journalist Paris Marx unpacks his new book "Hyperscale."
articles.body:
In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.

The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections . And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power .

In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”

“It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”

He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”

During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.

I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in?

Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so.

I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. And the thing that struck me most was the level of security.

Obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these big fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it.

Then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby.

It was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that.

Before I read your book, I thought of data centers as something that’s important, but a little bit boring. How did you decide they were interesting and rich enough to sustain an entire book?

I felt the same. I was aware that data centers had been out there, but it was not something that I was paying particularly close attention to. But then there were a number of stories that of tipped me off to the fact that there might be more here, and that it was worth looking deeper into what was going on — the first being hearing about the water pressures created by data centers in Chile around the capital of Santiago , where companies like Google and Microsoft were building data centers, and communities were concerned about their access to water and started organizing around that.

And then hearing about how much electricity data centers were consuming in Ireland, to the point that now they consume more than 20% of the country’s electricity , and that was obviously pushing up power prices. It was putting pressures on the grid, such that the grid operator actually put a moratorium in place for grid connections for data centers around the Dublin area, back in 2022. This was even before the generative AI moment that caused a surge in construction of data centers.

And then the other one was in The Dalles, Oregon, where Google had actually built its first company-owned data centers about 20 years back. In that case, its water deal was coming up for renewal. It wanted to build more data centers there, so it needed more water. And when the residents started asking, “How much water is Google actually using?” a journalist at The Oregonian went to the city and essentially asked, “Hey, how much water is Google using? Our readers would like to know this,” he was hit with a lawsuit instead of being given that information. Because Google did not want it to be public. And then, of course, when it did come out about a year later, Google revealed that it was using 29% of the city’s water, which seemed quite significant.

That was around when ChatGPT was being released and generative AI was starting to take off. It felt like, okay, there are these pockets of places where a lot of data centers have already been constructed, where they are putting pressures on the communities that are causing people to respond, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities. It was a good time to really start to dig in and pay attention.

You don’t just talk about the data centers’ environmental impact, but also, they [become] your way in to talk about this broader tech moment. They represent to you — particularly the hyperscale data centers — represent to you how these tech companies are doing business now.

Absolutely. The hyperscale data centers and just the scale of the construction — whether it’s the the size of the actual facilities themselves or the number that these companies are trying to build out, just feels fundamentally unsustainable.

They’re just demanding too much from the communities where they’re being located, whether that’s because of electricity or because of water use or what have you, or just the fact that they’re building out so many, that when you think about the cumulative impact and you look at the demand for water, but particularly for energy from fossil fuels, that means that it’s just completely out of line with a livable planet and an amount of computation that feels like it makes any degree of sense for us to have constructed.

I think it really goes back to the hubris of the tech industry and of these major tech companies and the tech billionaires that run them, and the fact that they have these particular visions of the future that are based on fantasies , but also on expanding their own power and influence over the world, and they don’t seem to mind that everyone else then has to pay the cost that comes with their ambitions and what they are seeking to do.

And I feel like it’s become particularly egregious with generative AI and the data centers to power them, where many of the benefits that were supposed to come of generative AI do not appear to have materialized — whether those are the economic benefits, the productivity benefits, but also the the benefits of delivery of services like healthcare and education to the public, as we heard Sam Altman saying a lot in the in the early days of ChatGPT.

Paired with that, there has been this massive environmental cost […] but there’s also this massive and growing social cost, when you think about the mental health impacts of chatbot dependence, of all the false information that pervades social media platforms now, of the deepfake crisis, and I could go on and on and on.

It’s not surprising that there has been backlash. But I have been surprised at how widespread it’s been, and also how bipartisan — you talk about Ron DeSantis and Bernie Sanders both being opposed to data centers. Why do you think it’s become such a unifying issue?

Because it’s not an abstract issue, right? I think even when we think about generative AI or social media or something like that, [it] can feel abstract. It’s a service that you access from your phone or from your computer. It’s not something that is tangible in the world.

But when a data center is coming to set up shop in your community, it’s very physical, it’s very material. It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on. You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water,. potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.

I think that there was already a pre-existing frustration with the tech industry that came from the quality of the products, the effects that they’re having on our society and our lives. For some people, [they have] frustration with the way that the tech industry has been collaborating with the Trump administration and with right-wing political groups in different parts of the world. But then you add on top of that the actual effects that come of having one of these infrastructures be planned or located in your community, and that anger gets kind of directed into that physical manifestation of this thing that you have an issue with.

Obviously, the data centers are at the forefront of this, and it’s what we pay the most attention to. But we also see this increasingly with other aspects of the tech industry, whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.

There’s a lot of frustration with the physical manifestations of the tech industry, because that is something that can really be felt more directly, but can also be challenged more directly. You can delete an app on your phone, but what difference does that really make to the company? It doesn’t often seem like very much.

The tech companies have reacted to this backlash in a few different ways. One is that Microsoft, Amazon, and OpenAI have all talked about [their commitment] that they’re not going to use NDAs anymore in their negotiations with local governments. How big a difference do you think that will make?

I do think it’s going to be good that it will be easier for people to access information on these projects that are being located in their communities. But part of the reason why we’re seeing these shifts is exactly in response to that opposition.

We’re seeing the tech companies propose to pay for more of the electricity infrastructure that will be required for their data centers to reduce the pressure on ratepayers, because people are angry about that. They’re promising to use different water-based cooling systems in their data centers, to say that they’re able to use less electricity.

When we look at the NDAs and the decision or the announcement that they’re not going to use those anymore, I think it’s also because it’s working against them. People know what a data center is now, and if people find out that a data center is coming to town and they have questions and they’re not getting answers, that’s only going to further fuel the opposition to those data centers.

So, it’s not really a surprise to see [the tech companies] do this, and it’s a way that they can get a positive PR thing by saying, “We’re not going to use these NDAs that are working against us anyway. “

One of the other ways they’ve responded is by saying that there’s a lot of misinformation about the environmental harms, or that they’re being overstated, or that they can mitigate them with renewable technology. How valid do you think those arguments are?

I think that the industry recognizes that there is a lot of concern and they’re trying to basically move into the discussion with narratives of their own to have people question whether data centers are really a problem or not.

I feel like we don’t see the industry doing as much on the energy side anymore, particularly on the fossil fuel side, because they realize that they have kind of lost that argument. If you look back a year and a half, two years ago, they were talking a lot about renewables , about nuclear energy, you don’t hear so much of that discourse anymore.

They have pivoted, instead, to focus on the water question, where I think that they feel that they can use more abstract national figures in order to confuse the public about what’s going on. They can say, “If you look nationally, agriculture and golf courses also use a lot of water. So you don’t need to be worried about a data center coming to tow,n because they don’t use as much, in aggregate.”

But the issue with data center water use is not a national issue. It’s a local issue. There are unquestionably going to be communities where they seek to locate data centers that are going to have plenty of water and that are not going to be concerned about a data center coming to town. But they’re also locating [data centers] in a lot of communities that are experiencing high degrees of water stress, which means that they don’t have the water to really provide to these infrastructures.

We have also seen them pivoting to move away from the evaporative cooling systems, the ones that require a lot of water — because you need to take in a certain amount of water as it gets too hot, it evaporates away, and so you can see why you need a consistent flow of water into the data center for that type of cooling system — to a closed loop system, where you basically have a certain amount of water, it stays within the data center, you keep cooling it down by using electricity to do that, and so you clearly don’t need as much water.

That is their new way to say, “Hey, don’t worry about the water use. We’re going to switch to this other system.” But the issue there, of course, is that it does require more electricity in order to keep that water cooled down, and that is often not part of what they talk about or discuss when they are proposing that as an alternative.

Then the other thing is that it’s not just water that is in those pipes or tubes going through the data center. There’s also a lot of coolant in there, a lot of chemicals, and communities where these projects are being located with closed loop cooling systems are becoming increasingly concerned about those coolants leaking out into their water supply and what that is going to mean.

In the book, you say repeatedly that you’re not against technology itself or even data centers in general, but [against] this hyperscale approach. The book is called “Hyperscale.” The last chapter is called “Human Scale.” Why do you see scale as such an important part of the problem?

Because scale is what creates the pressures, whether those are the pressures on the communities or you know the pressures on our wider electricity system and whatnot.

I don’t think that the inherent problem is data centers, because we have had data centers for a long time, and sure, there have been occasional concerns about specific projects, but data centers as a whole have not been an issue that the public has felt merited this degree of attention. So that is why I feel the hyperscale data center, and particularly the acceleration that we’ve seen in the expansion of the size of these hyperscale data centers, but also the number of data centers that these companies are building out, is notable in this moment.

Linked to that is not just the scale of the demand created by these hyperscale data centers, but also, what they are supposed to be powering? That is where the other disconnect lies. They’re demanding a lot, but if we were actually getting something good for it, this might be justified. I think that for a lot of people, and I feel like we see this reflected in polling, they’re not actually seeing the benefits from generative AI.

So then the question becomes: “Okay, we’re expending all of these resources, we’re pushing up emissions such that climate change is going to be accelerated just to build out all these data centers to meet the ambitions of generative AI that the tech companies have, but then we’re not actually getting much benefit out of that technology. So what are we actually doing here?”

One other thing that really struck a chord with me was your description about how tech executives often talk about the future as if there’s [just one] inevitable future. The only thing that’s in question is how quickly we arrive there [and] who’s going to make the most money off of it.

This is so important for me, because I do feel like how we think about the future then shapes decisions that we make. The tech billionaires, they see the future in a certain way […] and I think that they have been very successful in getting us to buy into their vision of the future for the past several decades. But that does not mean that that is the only way that the future has to be.

We can imagine a very different kind of future, and that would mean that we place our resources in different places and actually develop technology in a different way, toward different outcomes, with different incentives driving that work.

There are interesting conversations happening in different parts of the world right now around things like digital sovereignty, getting off of these technologies from the U.S. tech companies. But in some cases, those conversations are quickly captured by industry in those different parts of the world to say, “Okay, we want to get off U.S. technology, but let’s have our local companies do effectively the same thing, and just let them do the same exploitative practices and make the money that the U.S. tech companies would be making.” And I don’t think that that is the right way forward.

I also think that there is a role for public sector development of technology in a way that we’ve eschewed or even looked at skeptically for the past number of decades, because the idea was that technology had to be left to the private sector. What we’re starting to see in Europe is a bit more funding of public technology, in order to develop the services that government itself depends on, and I think that that is a good first step.

But especially when we’re looking at the Microsoft outage that happened just recently, and we’re looking at Google threatening schools with their access to Google search if they don’t accept Google AI tool, I think that there’s a real moment right now to put resources into developing something different, that doesn’t come from these major tech companies, and that hopefully can have much more public benefit than what these companies now provide us.

articles.title: Sam Altman’s OpenAI Foundation joins Rockefeller Foundation to launch $50 million AI initiative for cities, offering grants of up to $2 million for public services
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence is beginning to find a place in the everyday work of local governments, from tracking disease outbreaks to warning neighbourhoods
articles.body: Artificial intelligence is beginning to find a place in the everyday work of local governments, from tracking disease outbreaks to warning neighbourhoods about floods. Yet many cities lack the money, technical support and expertise needed to put such systems into practice. A new $50 million partnership between the OpenAI Foundation and the Rockefeller Foundation aims to address some of these gaps. Announced on October 14, 2026, the initiative will fund organisations working with city governments to introduce AI-based solutions to public services. Individual grants could reach $2 million, with projects expected to address problems affecting residents across different parts of the world.OpenAI and Rockefeller offer up to $2 million for city AI projectsCalled Cities Deliver: AI Solutions for Public Services, the programme will provide grants to eligible nonprofit and civil society organisations that collaborate with municipal authorities. The funding is intended for projects that use advanced AI systems to improve how cities deliver services, respond to local problems and reach residents.Grants will range from $500,000 to $2 million. The initiative aims to reach as many as 100 million city residents through the projects it supports. Applications opened on October 14 and are scheduled to close on November 29, 2026. Organisations that meet the initial requirements can submit proposals through a global open call, with those shortlisted moving to the next stage of selection.The programme is not restricted to organisations working in a particular country. Its focus is on finding solutions that can address practical public-service challenges and potentially be adapted by other cities.Four key areas targeted by the $50 million AI grants for citiesReportedly, the funding call identifies four broad areas for projects: public health, economic mobility, environmental resilience and civic engagement. Each covers a different set of responsibilities that local governments handle.In public health, proposals could involve disease monitoring, frontline healthcare, disability support, nutrition and improving access to food. Economic mobility projects may focus on helping unemployed or underemployed people find work, access benefits, develop skills or connect with employers. The intention is to use AI to make existing support systems easier for residents to navigate.Environmental resilience is another area of interest. Projects could help local authorities prepare for extreme weather, improve emergency responses, monitor energy infrastructure or manage land in vulnerable communities. Under civic engagement, the programme will consider systems that make it easier for residents to communicate with government departments, access court services, use digital platforms and participate in local decision-making. Projects connected to voting and elections are excluded.Earlier AI projects in Cali, Rio and Cape Town offer a blueprint for new grantsAs per The Rockefeller Foundation, the new funding initiative follows several years of work involving the two foundations and city leaders. Their collaboration can be traced to a 2023 gathering that brought together more than 40 civic leaders from six continents, alongside representatives from academia, philanthropy and nonprofit organisations. Discussions centred on the practical difficulties of bringing AI into local government, including the need for trained people, suitable technology and financial backing.The Rockefeller Foundation subsequently supported projects in Cali in Colombia, Cape Town in South Africa and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil. These initiatives have explored how AI could be used to address problems that local authorities were already dealing with.In Cali, an outbreak forecasting system known as Dengue.AI has been developed to help authorities anticipate dengue activity. According to the city's mayor, Alejandro Eder, the technology can provide warnings up to three weeks ahead, giving public health teams more time to prepare preventive measures. The work has been reported as benefiting a population of more than 2.2 million people. The Rockefeller Foundation now plans to support an expansion of the system from Cali to Cartagena.Rio de Janeiro has been working on an AI-assisted flood warning system, developed with Columbia University and supported by the Rockefeller Foundation. The project uses WhatsApp to communicate alerts and has focused on communities exposed to flooding, including Acari and Jardim Maravilha. The proposed expansion would extend the system to more residents and cover a wider range of extreme weather events.Cape Town has taken a different approach, developing a platform for communication between residents and municipal authorities. The system is designed to let people interact with the city in their own language, using voice messages or text through a platform they already use. The Rockefeller Foundation intends to help extend its reach within Cape Town and potentially beyond the city.What the two foundations want to achieveRockefeller Foundation president Dr Rajiv J. Shah said, “Over the past three years, we’ve seen what happens when city leaders, researchers, and local innovators build with AI around real problems. Cities Deliver takes what’s working in Cali, Cape Town, Rio, and elsewhere and opens it up to institutions everywhere, so more cities can benefit from the same kind of partnership.”Anna Makanju, head of civil society and philanthropy at the OpenAI Foundation, said, “Cities are on the front lines of some of the biggest challenges facing communities, and the organizations working alongside them understand what it takes to deliver solutions that work.”The initiative also comes against a backdrop of growing urban populations. United Nations estimates published in 2025 put the world's population at approximately 8.2 billion, with 45% living in cities. Local authorities are responsible for services that influence access to healthcare, employment, safety and public participation. However, the cost of implementation and concerns about protecting sensitive data can make the adoption of AI difficult for governments with limited resources.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available information from the OpenAI Foundation and The Rockefeller Foundation. articles.title: La IA plagia su trabajo para probar la Hipótesis de Riemann y manda 16 hojas quejándose al dueño de Claude: "Están privatizando el conocimiento humano"
articles.standfirst: Robert Edward Grant denuncia solapamientos entre su estudio geométrico y la prueba vinculada a Claude
articles.summary: Robert Edward Grant denuncia solapamientos entre su estudio geométrico y la prueba vinculada a Claude
articles.body: El debate sobre los límites éticos y legales de la inteligencia artificial (IA) suma un nuevo episodio. El investigador independiente Robert Edward Grant afirma que Claude podría haber plagiado su trabajo —publicado en enero de 2026 bajo el título Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis: A Geometric Constraint on Prime Fluctuations, donde plantea un enfoque geométrico basado en relaciones dimensionales y fluctuaciones de los números primos— para ayudar a probar la Hipótesis de Riemann. Aunque no ha sido hasta este mes de noviembre cuando ha trascendido que Grant ha escrito a Dario Amodei, director ejecutivo de Anthropic, con copia a asesores generales, aseguradoras de salida a bolsa y miembros de la junta, sobre las similitudes entre la demostración de Levent Alpöge y el enfoque que él estaba desarrollando de manera independiente. La carta completa de 16 páginas ha sido publicada en X. La controversia no es aislada dentro de la comunidad académica. Preguntas similares surgieron a principios de este año sobre el problema de Navier–Stokes y el contraejemplo a la conjetura de soficity de Gromov, donde en ambos casos varios matemáticos afirmaron que sus propias charlas podrían haber sido utilizadas para producir la demostración. Sin embargo, analistas como Valerio Capraro o Angela Rasmussen han abordado en redes la dificultad de auditar estos sistemas, señalando que "es prácticamente imposible determinar si una charla particular influyó en la respuesta de un modelo. Así que probablemente nunca sabremos si estas afirmaciones específicas son verdaderas o falsas". Más allá de la autoría concreta de estas pruebas, el trasfondo del conflicto apunta al modo en que se alimentan los algoritmos avanzados con material compartido en plataformas digitales. "Lo que se está volviendo cada vez más claro es que los laboratorios de IA están entrenando sus modelos con nuestras ideas en la frontera del conocimiento humano", advierten las voces críticas del entorno investigador, subrayando el vacío legal existente cuando se procesan hallazgos científicos recientes. Para quienes denuncian estas prácticas, el escenario resulta especialmente delicado por dos motivos fundamentales. "La primera tiene que ver con la propiedad intelectual. Si una idea que comparto en mi charla aparece en tu demostración, ¿dónde trazamos la línea entre lo que es mío y lo que es tuyo?", plantean los afectados ante la ausencia de criterios que diferencien la inspiración del aprovechamiento indebido en el aprendizaje automático. El segundo argumento apunta directamente al modelo de negocio de las grandes tecnológicas del sector. "La segunda es aún más preocupante. Los laboratorios de IA de vanguardia nos venden nuestro propio conocimiento a través de suscripciones de pago", denuncian, concluyendo con una advertencia sobre el futuro del acceso abierto a la ciencia: "Están literalmente privatizando el conocimiento colectivo humano".

articles.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development | TechCrunch
articles.summary: To establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how to measure speed.
articles.body:
A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.

Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”

But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement.

In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.”

Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.

“GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.”

So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.”

articles.title: Faculdades Senac Curitiba oferecem graduação e pós com descontos | G1

articles.summary: Com 80 anos de experiência, Senac PR abre vagas para 2027 nas áreas de Gastronomia, Estética e Tecnologia, com ensino prático, bolsas e condições especiais.
articles.body:
Investir em qualificação é um passo importante para conquistar oportunidades profissionais. As Faculdades de Tecnologia Senac Curitiba estão com inscrições abertas para os cursos de graduação e pós-graduação de 2027, nas unidades Centro e Portão. Com uma metodologia que une teoria, prática, inovação e humanização, a instituição prepara profissionais para os desafios de um mercado em constante transformação.

São 80 anos de experiência do Senac em educação profissional, com uma proposta de ensino que valoriza a aplicação do conhecimento, o desenvolvimento de competências e a conexão com o mundo do trabalho.

Nas Faculdades Senac, o aprendizado vai além da sala de aula. As atividades são planejadas para aproximar os estudantes das situações que encontrarão em suas carreiras, incentivando a resolução de problemas, a criatividade, o empreendedorismo e o uso de novas tecnologias.

Outro diferencial é a possibilidade de escolher formações que atendem a diferentes momentos da vida profissional. Enquanto os cursos de graduação representam a oportunidade de conquistar um diploma de Ensino Superior e desenvolver competências para ingressar ou avançar no mercado, as especializações permitem aprofundar conhecimentos, ampliar a área de atuação e buscar novas posições na carreira.

Graduação para começar ou transformar sua carreira

As Faculdades Senac PR oferecem cursos superiores de tecnologia para diferentes perfis profissionais. Em Curitiba, as opções são:

Curitiba Centro: Tecnologia em Gastronomia (vespertino e noturno) e Tecnologia em Estética e Cosmética (noturno).

Curitiba Portão: Tecnologia em Análise e Desenvolvimento de Sistemas (noturno).

Na Faculdade Senac Curitiba Centro, o curso superior de Tecnologia em Gastronomia oferece uma experiência de aprendizagem que combina conhecimentos teóricos com atividades práticas, estimulando o desenvolvimento de habilidades fundamentais para a atuação profissional.

A formação é uma alternativa tanto para quem deseja ingressar no universo gastronômico quanto para profissionais que já trabalham na área e buscam aperfeiçoamento e qualificação acadêmica.

Já o curso superior de Tecnologia em Estética e Cosmética propõe uma formação que integra conhecimentos científicos, técnicos e práticos, preparando os estudantes para os diferentes desafios da área.

A proposta educacional valoriza o desenvolvimento de competências para a atuação profissional, o acompanhamento das inovações do setor e a capacidade de oferecer serviços com responsabilidade e qualidade.

O curso superior de Tecnologia em Análise e Desenvolvimento de Sistemas, oferecido pela Faculdade Senac Curitiba Portão, é voltado à formação de profissionais capazes de compreender necessidades, desenvolver soluções e atuar com tecnologias aplicadas a diferentes contextos.

A graduação possibilita o desenvolvimento de conhecimentos relacionados à programação, análise de sistemas, desenvolvimento de software e resolução de problemas por meio da tecnologia.

Além das competências técnicas, a proposta de formação também valoriza o raciocínio lógico, o trabalho em equipe, a criatividade e a capacidade de adaptação às constantes transformações do setor.

O ingresso pode ser realizado por vestibular gratuito, com avaliação presencial agendada ou remota, nota do Enem, transferência ou segunda graduação, conforme os critérios do edital. As aulas começam em 15 de fevereiro de 2027.

Pós-graduação para avançar profissionalmente

Para quem já possui diploma superior, a pós-graduação do Senac é uma oportunidade de aprofundar conhecimentos, valorizar o currículo e ampliar as possibilidades de atuação, com início das aulas em 8 de março de 2027.

Conquistar um diploma de graduação representa uma etapa importante da trajetória acadêmica e profissional. No entanto, em um mercado marcado por mudanças rápidas, a formação continuada ganha cada vez mais relevância.

Para profissionais que desejam assumir funções de liderança, migrar para áreas em expansão, empreender ou aprimorar a atuação em seus setores, a especialização pode representar um passo estratégico.

Além de agregar uma nova qualificação ao currículo, a pós-graduação oferece oportunidades de atualização, contato com ferramentas utilizadas pelas empresas e desenvolvimento de projetos que aproximam o aprendizado da realidade profissional.

O conhecimento especializado também pode contribuir para a tomada de decisões, a identificação de soluções inovadoras e o desenvolvimento de uma visão mais abrangente dos negócios.

Duas especializações estão disponíveis em Curitiba:

Ciência de Dados com IA Aplicada — Curitiba Portão: formação voltada ao uso de Inteligência Artificial, análise de dados, automação e ferramentas como Python, SQL e Power BI para desenvolver soluções estratégicas.

Gestão de Negócios Gastronômicos — Curitiba Centro: integra Gastronomia, empreendedorismo, gestão financeira, marketing e inovação para preparar profissionais para liderar e desenvolver negócios no setor de alimentação.

Por que escolher uma graduação ou pós-graduação no Senac?

A escolha de uma instituição de Ensino Superior envolve diferentes fatores. Além do curso e da localização, é importante considerar a qualidade da formação, a estrutura disponível, a metodologia utilizada e a conexão do aprendizado com as exigências do mercado de trabalho.

Nas Faculdades Senac Curitiba, esses elementos fazem parte de uma proposta educacional que valoriza a aplicação prática dos conhecimentos e a formação integral dos estudantes.

Experiência em educação profissional: são 80 anos de atuação do Senac no Brasil, contribuindo para a formação e o desenvolvimento de profissionais de diferentes setores.

Metodologia que une teoria e prática: atividades que aproximam os conteúdos acadêmicos de situações reais do cotidiano profissional.

Inovação e tecnologia: utilização de ferramentas, recursos e metodologias conectados às transformações do mundo do trabalho.

Formação humanizada: desenvolvimento de competências técnicas e comportamentais, valorizando a ética, a colaboração e o relacionamento interpessoal.

Estrutura para experiências práticas: ambientes de aprendizagem que permitem colocar em prática os conhecimentos adquiridos durante a formação.

Conexão com o mercado: projetos, desafios e atividades que estimulam o pensamento crítico, a criatividade e a capacidade de solucionar problemas.

Educação Flexível: combina aulas presenciais, atividades práticas e estudos em ambiente virtual. O formato facilita a conciliação entre trabalho e formação, mantendo o contato com professores e experiências reais de aprendizagem.

Para facilitar o acesso ao Ensino Superior, as Faculdades Senac oferecem condições especiais:

80% de desconto na primeira mensalidade para matrículas até 15/01/2027.

50% na primeira mensalidade entre 16/01 e 01/02/2027.

20% de desconto por pontualidade, conforme as condições vigentes.

80% de desconto na primeira mensalidade até 15/01/2027.

20% por pontualidade e benefícios para comerciários e ex-alunos, conforme regulamento.

Seja para conquistar o primeiro diploma ou investir em uma especialização, as Faculdades Senac Curitiba oferecem formação conectada às necessidades do mercado, com a experiência de quem há 80 anos contribui para o desenvolvimento profissional no Brasil.

articles.title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.summary: AI employees in the industry's epicentre - San Francisco - worry that the sector is overheated.
articles.body:
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.

Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.

Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.

The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it s now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.

Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.

Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up in San Francisco.

Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).

Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal

Wealthy AI workers send San Francisco house prices soaring

Follow the money: Who pays for the AI boom now?

What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.

He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.

But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"

Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.

"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."

If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.

That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.

But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.

For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".

Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.

"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.

Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.

But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing, which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.

"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.

All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.

"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."

As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

articles.title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
articles.summary: Three significant backers share what gave them conviction to bet billions on Anthropic.
articles.body:
When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history.

But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year.

“We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch.

Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said.

Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times.

Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win.

Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation.

“Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials.

Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch.

After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said.

“It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations.

articles.title: IIM Bangalore’s talent is better than it thinks
articles.summary: Arun Chandrasekhar describes IIM Bangalore’s faculty as “extremely good”.
articles.body: Arun Chandrasekhar describes IIM Bangalore’s faculty as “extremely good”. He was particularly struck by the number of research assistants, including undergraduates already doing serious research and preparing for graduate study.But he noticed something that concerned him. Some of the students he spoke to had interesting research ideas and strong backgrounds, yet were cautious about applying to top global universities and research programmes. He told them: apply anyway.Chandrasekhar is a Stanford professor, an economist who has spent much of his career studying poverty and development in India. He was born and raised in the US, but his family is from Bengaluru. He won the Infosys Prize 2024 in economics, and used his sabbatical to deepen links between IIMB and the research lab he runs in Bengaluru.“I was talking to some of the students about where they had applied for postdoc or graduate school, and they are from smart backgrounds, have interesting research ideas, but they're like, shy about the scope of their applications than I would have imagined,” he says, and notes the iconic phrase coined by Wayne Gretzky, the Canadian former professional ice hockey player: “You miss 100% of the shots you don’t take.”He told them they should apply to a number of places they're not considering. “Because everything is low chance for everybody, but you have really interesting stuff here, and if you get in, the returns are very steep, and if you don't, that's okay,” he says.The problem, he says, may be lack of information – about what opportunities exist, what scholarships are available or how institutions assess applicants.One student particularly impressed him. The student had independently learned Lean, a programming language used to formally verify mathematical proofs, to pursue an interest in game theory. Chandrasekhar says he had never encountered someone who was not yet in graduate school but had independently gone that far in learning a specialised research tool. “It's a real achievement and you should take this and run with it,” was his message to the student.Building connections helps everyoneChandrasekhar was particularly impressed by IIMB’s behavioural economics lab, which allows researchers to conduct controlled experiments in simulated markets and games using specialised software, computers and physical infrastructure.He sees an opportunity to build more links between this and his own work, including his Bengaluru lab. Chandrasekhar is part of the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, or J-PAL, a global research centre founded in 2003 at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) by Nobel laureates Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo with the objective of reducing global poverty by ensuring that policy decisions are rooted in rigorous scientific evidence. It’s today a global network that helps researchers build field laboratories, recruit research staff, work with local partners and conduct development research.For development economics, that local context matters. Chandrasekhar is conscious of being an outsider even though he has worked on the country for years. IIMB, he says, can gain access to international research networks and infrastructure, while researchers outside India can gain from local knowledge, students and faculty. His lab has already begun exploring collaborative work in areas including skilling, technology and AI.Chandrasekhar says universities need not work in isolation from policy organisations, research networks and institutions that have built expertise in conducting field research. Connecting those pieces, he suggests, can give students more exposure, researchers more resources, and policymakers better evidence.One of the things we do a lot (in Stanford), especially the younger faculty, is spend a lot of time not just socialising, but really picking at each other's research from different fields. You and I as friends, we might go and play basketball together or have a drink together, but at the same time, you, as a macroeconomist, may have modeled individual behaviour in a certain way, which is really strange to me as a person who works on psychology, and we discuss it, and then may eventually even decide to work together on it. But I think the economics faculty there (IIM-B) was more siloed. I was like, you guys should do more of this (interdisciplinary discussions). Because there's so much complementarity.Arun Chandrasekhar, Professor of Economics, Stanford UniversityFearless legend or grounded realist?
