articles.title: Meta AI head Alexandr Wang warns about AI; says: Superintelligence is coming, but how 'dangerous' it will be depends on humans as ...
articles.summary: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang has issued a serious warning about the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, saying that the world may already be entering
articles.body: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang has issued a serious warning about the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, saying that the world may already be entering the era of superintelligence. In a lengthy post shared on social media platform X (formerly known As Twitter) Wang said that next year could prove critical in determining whether increasingly powerful AI systems benefit humanity or lead to outcomes that are difficult for humans to control. The comments made by Wang come amid the growing debate within technology industry over the pace of the development of AI. He also acknowledged the potential of AI in accelerating scientific and economic progress. He further emphasised that humanity must remain actively involved in shaping its future rather than enabling the society to be handed over to machines.Alexandr Wang: ’Superintelligence is coming’In his post, Wang declared that "superintelligence is arriving" and argued that recent AI breakthroughs suggest machines are rapidly approaching, and in some areas surpassing, the highest levels of human intellectual performance. He pointed to the reported proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, as a milestone that demonstrates the scale of change underway. Wang described the achievement as an intellectual accomplishment unlike anything humanity has seen before and said it showcased the capabilities of what he referred to as an "alien mind" that humans do not fully understand.According to Wang, the development marks a turning point similar to the moment AI models began solving highly difficult American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) problems, signalling that raw intelligence was no longer the primary limitation for advanced AI systems.AI moving beyond human expertiseWang argued that many of the toughest mathematical challenges are more intellectually demanding than most real-world tasks performed by engineers, cybersecurity experts or business professionals. He feels that the as the capabilities of AI have improved, the practical limitations have been reduced and the AI models have also become quite effective across coding, cybersecurity and other sectors. He also emphasised that the remaining obstacles for AI systems are mainly related to the domain knowledge, experimentation and implementation rather than intelligence itself. Wang feels that as a result, AI is expected to become a main contributor to growth across almost every field of human activity."The remaining gaps for models to greatly surpass humanity in every field are no longer intelligence," he wrote, suggesting that future systems could significantly outperform the best human experts in many disciplines.What he expects nextWang said the remaining obstacles to AI surpassing humans in every field are domain know-how, infrastructure and experimentation, not intelligence. He concluded that AI will likely become the largest contributor to progress in nearly every field, outperforming the best humans. That includes AI research itself, which he called less demanding than the Riemann Hypothesis. Models, he said, will be smart enough to automate all of it and to improve themselves in a clearly superhuman way, while speeding up biological, weapons and economics research. He warned that fields could advance faster than humans can understand or monitor.A call for a different pathWang said it is hard to imagine humanity keeping control over unconstrained recursive self-improvement, or over a superintelligence 1,000 times smarter than people in every field. He argued the scientific and technical problems of capability progress are likely solved, so the urgent work is safety, alignment and security, along with deciding how progress should unfold. He criticized what he called lazy thinking in the AI industry: the idea that superintelligence is inevitable and only doing it safely remains. Society should not accept handing itself over to AI, he said, and should aim for technology that gives all humans greater agency. That likely requires the whole industry to depart from the default path, he added.Read Alexandr Wang’s complete post hereSuperintelligence is arriving. How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in. As someone who has spent much of my life in math and science, I see the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as clearly marking the beginning of a significant change. For most who have studied math, this represents the absolute pinnacle of intellectual accomplishment—nothing humanity has ever accomplished compares to proving the Riemann Hypothesis in terms of sheer intellectual might and strength. As someone who grew up in Los Alamos, New Mexico, many physicists would agree that the discovery of the atomic bomb is a homework problem compared to the Riemann Hypothesis. It is hard to overstate the magnitude of discovery that we have just witnessed—completed with the help of an alien mind that we don’t understand.For those who did math competitions, there was a similar moment of “oh shit everything is about to change” when the models began acing the AIME in December 2024 with o3. The hardest AIME problems are much harder in terms of sheer intellectual difficulty than the problems that even the most advanced engineers and business people need to solve on a day-to-day basis. There of course is domain-specific knowledge, context, know-how, and other tactical constraints that were needed to unlock the models across other areas, but lack of raw intelligence was not the bottleneck. And in fact, the progress across other domains over the past 2 years as we’ve mitigated these non-intelligence factors has been immense—we have seen coding be nearly solved, the emergence of extremely powerful cyber capabilities, and strong agentic capabilities which have enabled the models to become general-purpose useful aides.Again the key insight here was simply that the hardest AIME problems are intellectually very difficult, far more difficult than most coding work, most cyber work, most business work, etc., and over the past two years we have been filling in the gaps to enable the models to accomplish those things.To be clear, AIME is an extracurricular activity for teenagers; the Riemann Hypothesis may be the most intellectually demanding problem humanity has ever devised, which some of the most brilliant humans over the past 150 years have dedicated their lives to. At MIT, my professors would have said the hardest intellectual problems in nearly every major field of human study are “easier” than the Riemann Hypothesis, albeit with other challenges such as experimentation, data, and feedback loops. The remaining gaps for models to greatly surpass humanity in every field are no longer intelligence; they are domain-specific know-how, plumbing, and experimentation. This means it is likely that AI will become the greatest contributor of progress across nearly every field, vastly outperforming the best humans.Notably, this is likely true of AI research. Most researchers would agree that AI research is certainly much less intellectually demanding than solving the Riemann Hypothesis. The models are clearly going to be intelligent enough to automate all of AI research and be clearly superhuman at improving themselves—along with massively accelerating biological research, weapons research, economics research, and more. The implications are enormous. In the same way that the math community has not fully digested the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, nearly every field could be accelerated at a pace beyond what humans can understand or monitor.It is now incredibly important for us to be thoughtful about the future we want and how we get there. It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement. It is equally hard to imagine a world where humanity maintains control with superintelligence that is 1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field. Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.I notice a particular form of lazy thinking within the AI industry, which is that ASI is inevitable and the only problem to solve is how to do it safely, but there is much more at stake. We should not be okay with a “handover” of society to AI. We should endeavor ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment. I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.body: As the Americans can preparing to travel for Thanksgiving, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has warned that the disruptions in technology may continue as companies and government agencies are modernising their systems for the age of artificial intelligence. Appearing on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Clayton said outages may continue as companies and the government upgrade their systems to adapt to the AI era. He said the public should expect heavy investment in upgrading systems and in cybersecurity, and that any major leap in technology, in computing power or applications, brings disruption. People should understand that systems will be upgraded and may be interrupted for a time, he said, and that companies and the government are dealing with the problem proactively.Americans should be prepared for disruptionsSpeaking on CNN's State of the Union, Clayton said the public should expect temporary interruptions as organisations invest heavily in new technologies and cybersecurity measures. "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Clayton said, according to a CNBC report.He added that people should understand that system upgrades may occasionally result in service interruptions while both government agencies and private companies work to strengthen infrastructure and security. "You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot," he said.What happenedGovernment officials have largely dismissed the idea that the outages are linked to a coordinated cyberattack or one driven by artificial intelligence. The disruptions also slowed some bank transactions.A technology failure triggered a nationwide ground stop for flights just over a week ago that lasted for hours. The Federal Aviation Administration said router upgrades produced a flood of data that caused the stoppage, and that there is no indication of a cyberattack. Microsoft separately said its Outlook outage resulted from an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade.Treasury secretary compares upgrades to a vaccineUS Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent delivered a similar message during an appearance on CBS' Face the Nation, urging Americans not to worry about the security of their financial institutions. Asked whether consumers should be concerned about banks, Bessent replied, "No, they shouldn't."Referring to software updates and security improvements designed to protect systems against emerging AI-related threats, he acknowledged that occasional glitches may occur."The patches may cause a glitch," Bessent said. "I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine; your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency."Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.summary: Just days after AI giant Anthropic made its highly anticipated stock market debut, one of its mathematicians made an announcement that could have
articles.body: Just days after AI giant Anthropic made its highly anticipated stock market debut, one of its mathematicians made an announcement that could have far-reaching implications for both artificial intelligence and mathematics: he believes that he has solved the 167-year-old Riemann Hypothesis with the help of Anthropic's AI model, Claude. As reported by Wall Street Journal, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, recently revealed that he has created a proof for the Riemann Hypothesis, one of the most famous and elusive unsolved problems in mathematics, using assistance from Claude. If the proof withstands scrutiny from the mathematical community, it would mark one of the most significant achievements in the history of the field and a major milestone for artificial intelligence.Why it matters, if it holdsProposed in 1859, the hypothesis has defeated mathematicians for 167 years and is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems. If the proof checks out, it would be the second of those problems solved with AI, after an OpenAI model, supported by millions of dollars in computing power, solved one in September. Humans alone have solved only one. For decades, mathematicians have viewed the problem as the discipline's "holy grail." Even advanced AI systems had previously failed to produce a complete proof. According to the report, Alpöge now believes that barrier has been broken.Claude's role in the proofAlpöge disclosed the findings saying the solution was reached with assistance from Claude. If verified, the breakthrough would become the second Millennium Prize Problem solved with the help of artificial intelligence, following an earlier AI-assisted breakthrough involving an OpenAI model.The mathematician published the proof using Lean, a formal programming language designed to enable computers to verify mathematical arguments line by line. By releasing the proof publicly, he invited mathematicians worldwide to examine and validate the work.A 250,000-page AI-generated argumentOne of the most interesting aspects of the claim is the size of the proof produced by Alpöge. He stressed that the complete argument is "incredibly long," and described the AI-generated version as a "massive unreadable travesty of slop." As reported by WSJ, the AI-generated proof has more than 250,000 pages. The length of the proof also underlines both the power and limitations of modern AI-assisted mathematics. Where a machine can easily navigate through vast chains of reasoning, understanding and cross checking the arguments still remain a significant challenge for human researchers.The record breaking IPO of AnthropicAnthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, above its marketed range of $70 to $78. The offering raised $81.3 billion, the largest on record, and values the company at about $1.5 trillion. Shares opened at $111.50 and rose to nearly $115. They closed 17.07% above the IPO price, then slipped 4.70% in after-hours trading. About 832 million shares changed hands, more than SpaceX’s first-day volume, making Anthropic the most actively traded stock on the Nasdaq.Amazon and Google parent Alphabet are major investors. After the IPO, Amazon will reportedly hold 14.7% and Alphabet 13.7%, with Alphabet’s stake including $10 billion of shares bought in a private placement alongside the offering. Both companies also supply computing and other infrastructure to Anthropic.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: NOOSHEEN HASHEMI: America's AI leadership needs more than one man
articles.summary: Nvidia's board says it won't reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, leaving founders and co-investors waiting to learn which AI funding rounds it will still lead.
articles.body: America’s AI industry is about to find out how much of its financing depended on Jensen Huang’s word.Huang has said he would be willing to return to Nvidia. On Tuesday, board chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO. For independent companies raising money now, the question is whether Nvidia will still commit early enough to bring other investors into their rounds.According to PitchBook, rounds Nvidia joined accounted for 27.2% of global venture deal value through mid-November. That includes every investor’s contribution, and a handful of very large rounds drove much of the total. Nvidia separately reported $99 billion in equity investments as of July 26. That was the value of its holdings at the time. We don’t know how much Nvidia put into independent open-model developers or how often it led their rounds. Reflection AI shows what Nvidia could do when it chose to lead. Huang reportedly committed Nvidia to half of Reflection’s initial $1 billion target and urged other investors to join. The round grew to $2 billion, and Nvidia put in about $800 million. It was an unusually large deal. The sequence is important: Huang committed Nvidia’s money first, then brought other investors in. Nvidia stood to sell chips to Reflection, and that kind of financing deserves scrutiny. It also shows why a lead investor’s decision canshape a round. Nvidia still has the means to invest. On Tuesday it reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, up 103% from a year earlier. Its board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap to continue without interruption. Interim CEO Colette Kress said the company is scrutinizing future investments, commitments and guarantees. She also said Nvidia had made no change to the financing conditions on its existing agreements with specialist cloud providers. I expect Nvidia to be more selective about taking new risks. The question for founders and co-investors is which deals it will still lead and how quickly it will decide. JENSEN HUANG’S NVIDIA DEBACLE REVEALS AMERICA’S REAL PROBLEM: NO SKILLED BUILDERS As an AI founder and investor, I see how quickly a delay can become a problem for a smaller company. Microsoft, Meta and Google can fund much of their own expansion. An independent lab can have payingcustomers and still need to raise money to train its next model. A specialist cloud provider has to finance the chips before it can sell the computing time. If the lead investor waits, others can wait too. The company still has to decide whether it can afford to reserve the computing capacity or keep the people it hired to do the work. China is already competing for the customers those companies could serve. The Lowy Institute counted nearly 1.8 billion downloads of Chinese models on Hugging Face in the third quarter, compared with 500 million for American models. Huawei shows customers how to run Alibaba’s Qwen on its Ascend chips. As more developers use Qwen, Huawei has a chance to sell them the systems that run it. Beijing’s AI action plan promotes both open-source cooperation and computing infrastructure abroad. That combination could become the next chapter of China’s Digital Silk Road. BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN Governments that want to run AI on their own infrastructure should have a competitive American choice in models and hardware. That means Nvidia and AMD, Broadcom’s custom accelerators and systems from specialists such as Cerebras and d-Matrix. Once a government buys the equipment, adapts its software and trains its engineers, switching suppliers is expensive. Americans can disagree about which chips Nvidia should be allowed to sell to China. Weakening Nvidia or the American companies that build with its technology would give Beijing an advantage while other countries are making those choices. Nvidia should continue backing independent AI companies. Kress and Jones should tell founders and co-investors who can approve pending deals, when decisions will come and whether Nvidia intends to provide follow-on financing. Institutional investors, sovereign wealth funds and independent venture firms should start putting together rounds of their own. Elon Musk, who has welcomed the idea of hiring Huang, could bring investors together for one such partnership. It would need firm capital commitments and the freedom to make investment decisions independently of xAI and his other companies. If we make a model’s weights public, Beijing can get them too. Our allies also need American models they can run on their own infrastructure, with their own data and under their own rules. If we leave that market to China, we make it easier for Beijing to sell the systems those countries will depend on for years. Before taxpayers guarantee financing for an open-model project, an independent review should establish which U.S. security interest it serves and whether the benefits of releasing the weights justify the risks. CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN I believe private investors should decide which companies deserve their money. I would make a narrow exception when a documented financing gap threatens a viable project vital to national security. The Treasury should convene private investors this week to find out which projects are at risk and how much private capital is ready to move. I would set an initial target of $100 billion in combined public and private commitments. Congress should act urgently to authorize a temporary federal credit guarantee under bipartisan oversight, drawing on the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital. Congress shouldseparately cap taxpayer exposure and set an expiration date. An independent committee should apply published criteria, require recusals for conflicts and approve guarantees only where private investors keep their own capital at risk. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP If Nvidia and private investors fill the gaps, the guarantees can go unused. It could take months to learn which deals will proceed. A lab can lose the team it took years to assemble in weeks. Nvidia can give founders answers now, and the Treasury can bring investors together while there are still deals to do.Disclosure: The author has an indirect investment in Reflection AI through her limited-partner interest in a fund managed by 1789 Capital.

Tomorrow, on Tuesday November 24th, the retail giant will roll out a live implementation of the Agent Gateway it announced last month, which helps AI agents find relevant products for you without sharing your purchase history, according to Walmart. Muse can make purchases through Walmart’s “Agent Profiles,” which provide a dedicated space for agent activity within your Walmart customer account. These profiles also allow you to set spending limits, approve purchases, and check the purchase history of everything bought by Muse. While other online retailers like Amazon and eBay have blocked AI agents from browsing their platforms, Walmart says that support for Meta’s Muse is “just the beginning,” and that additional Walmart shopping experiences for other AI agents and apps are “on the way.” Here are Walmart’s instructions for shopping its website via Muse: > 1. Tell Muse what you need. For example, ask it to find a great TV deal or show you which Walmart Black Friday deals are available for delivery. Muse can help you explore products and build your basket. > 2. Set your shopping rules. Muse will take you to Walmart to sign in, then bring you back to Muse. The first time you add an item to your cart, you’ll set up your Agent Profile on Walmart within your Walmart account, including a spending limit you’re comfortable with. > 3. Check out. Complete your purchase within the conversation using a card saved in your Walmart account, with the same Walmart prices you’d find on Walmart.com. And if something isn’t quite right, Walmart’s return policy still applies. Update, November 23rd: Walmart informed The Verge after publication that the Agent Gateway launch has been delayed by 24 hours. The ability to shop on Walmart via Muse will now be available on November 24th.

articles.title: Tesla Makes an Unsafe Pitch to Senior Drivers Clinging to Car Keys
articles.summary: The company is increasingly promoting its driver-assistance features to aging consumers.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Since getting a Model Y three years ago, Craig Johnson has become something of an evangelist for Tesla Inc. ( TSLA ).

The gas savings are nice, as is the charging network. But the real draw ended up being the system Tesla markets as Full Self-Driving.

Johnson, 73, sees Tesla's driver-assistance features as an ideal way to preserve or restore a measure of freedom for seniors. The Phoenix resident and IT consultant encourages friends in their 70s and 80s, including some with visual and mobility challenges, to test his SUV. He said he envisions a day when Teslas become known as "an old man's car."

Tesla warns consumers that FSD requires drivers to pay attention and be prepared to take immediate action at all times. It acknowledges none of its driver-assistance features make Teslas autonomous. And yet the company is increasingly promoting the merits of the system to seniors, further muddling the already complex question of when the moment has come for older drivers to give up their car keys.

Experts say the technology's limitations may actually raise risks for the elderly. The pitfalls of aging, including changes in vision, loss of physical mobility and slower reflexes, can impair an older driver's ability to safely take control when needed.

"You have to wait for it to make a mistake, notice it's making a mistake, and then react," said Philip Koopman, an autonomous vehicle researcher and emeritus professor at Carnegie Mellon University. That task takes more time than "just reacting if you're already paying attention."

Since June 2025, Tesla has reported almost 2,400 crashes where its advanced driver-assistance systems were engaged. In 24 of those collisions, at least one person died. In almost 2,300 of those crashes, the highest injury severity was reported as unknown to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. That means the carmaker likely did not have information about whether anyone was hurt in the crash, or how badly.

The data doesn't include drivers' ages, and there are no comprehensive statistics on the number of crashes involving the elderly using automated-driving systems.

But there are signs the technology is emerging as a risk for older drivers.

articles.title: Is Slough among areas seeing too many hyperscale AI data centres?
articles.summary: Is it time to slow the rollout of hyperscale AI data centres?
articles.body:
If you're a data centre geek you could fly to Virginia, USA, the only place you'll find more of them. Or you could head to Slough, home to the UK's data centre industry.

These centres have been working quietly in the background for more than 25 years. Until recently they received little attention.

The rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has changed that and the industry is now building more and much bigger data centres to cope with extra demand for the technology.

Campaigners in Slough want the government to slow down the roll-out of the new breed of much larger so-called hyperscale data centres with ministers saying the growth of AI is key to the country's economic future.

AI is everywhere. Like it or not it's already a part of our every day lives. In its simplest terms AI data centres are where the internet lives.

The people who run them like James Tyler, the managing director of Slough based firm Equinix says they bring thousands of jobs with them:

'In every data centre there'll be engineers and facilities experts who we employ directly. There's a whole supply chain that supports the design, build and operation of this entire industry. '

Equinix have been operating data centres in the east Berkshire town since the end of the last century. It does not operate its own AI computing hubs, rather it hires its buildings out to companies needing somewhere safe and secure to house their own AI computer servers.

Its data centres are powered entirely by renewables. But that's not true of all data centres. Some of the new generation of hyperscale AI facilities planned for areas in and around towns like Slough need so much power they can't yet to be hooked up to the electricity grid.

Chris Hilson is a professor of economic law at the University of Reading: "What they're planning to do is build what are essentially fossil fuel driven power sources and those will be burning fossil fuels and releasing CO2 into the atmosphere for a number of years."

The data centre industry says it is committed to using renewables wherever possible but argues that the lack of capacity in the country's electricity grid means it can't just sit on its hands and wait years to be connected while other countries like China and America forge ahead.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) previously told the BBC emissions from data centres "are factored into our modelling.

"We will set out Carbon Budget 7 by June 2026, in line with our statutory duties," a DESNZ spokesperson said.

The government must set this budget by June this year, as part of its legally binding commitment to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

Back in Slough there's a growing awareness of just how many data centres are springing up there. As the town's trading estate runs out of space and new ones grow ever bigger some are being built on the very edge of residential areas.

Dr Ambily Banerjee runs a campaign group called Slough Against Data Centres. She says: "You can not miss the sheer size of these monstrosities. What we're saying is we do care about our communities.

"Can we please have some accountability from our elected officials and from our government, to look at the impact in a place like Slough which already has so many data centres, before you start doing this across the country."

The UK's economy grew at its fastest rate in three years in the most recent quarter of this year with analysts saying AI businesses were key to this growth.

In last month's Budget the government said it wanted more data centres opened but only if the industry signed up to a covenant encouraging it to work more closely with local communities.

Dr Banerjee was and remains deeply unimpressed:

'I think the government needs to be embarassed about the covenant because they talk a lot about residents and the benefits for residents withour producing a single line about how they're going to engage with us.'

There are already more than 500 data centres dotted around the country with another 150 in the pipeline. Slough with its proximity to London and an already extensive network of fibre optic cables embedded in its trading estate is well placed to profit from what some are dubbing a 21st Century gold rush.

articles.title: Nvidia reverses course and brings Jensen Huang back as CEO
articles.summary: The stunning reversal was supported by senior officials in the U.S. government.
articles.body:
In a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board said on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, less than two weeks after he resigned following his admission of at least two extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman whom the U.S. government suspects to be a Chinese spy.

The decision marks an extraordinary comeback for one of the tech industry’s most influential executives, whose abrupt departure raised questions about national security and the future of the world’s most valuable chipmaker.

Notably, the U.S. government itself played a role in his return: Nvidia’s board said it consulted senior government officials before determining that Huang posed no national security risk.

In the days since Huang resigned, President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his support for the ousted executive, who is now back at the helm of the AI chip giant. A long list of high-profile tech executives have also pushed the board to bring Huang back, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan — all of whom signed a petition pushing for reinstatement.

The company said the board’s unanimous decision followed a series of discussions and meetings with Huang, after which they were “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”

Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones said they didn’t intend reinstate Huang. Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.

Jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view. In a prepared statement, Jones said the board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.

“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company,” Jones said. “We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer.”

In a statement, Huang said he was honored to return to his role as the head of the company he co-founded in 1993.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said. “I want to thank the Nvidia Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading Nvidia during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

articles.title: The return of massive attacks of disruption and destruction
articles.summary: The most immediate threat comes from us: people and governments.
articles.body:
More than a decade ago, I predicted that the overriding danger to international order and stability was not great power conflict, terrorism or even a failed government, but massive attacks of disruption and destruction . Whether acts of man or of nature such as pandemics, catastrophic weather or environmental events.

This is more than self-evident today. It is not only floods, fires and earthquakes that have brought calamity across the globe. It could also be extreme climate change, if it accelerates or is not contained.

However, the most immediate threat comes from us: people and governments. Since 1945, nuclear and then thermonuclear weapons — the latter measured in megatons , not kilotons, of destructive power — have posed an apocalyptic threat to humankind. If war were to go thermonuclear and global, no winners would be left — possibly only survivors depending on the extent of destruction and the effects of radiation. Plutonium, the mater of choice in these weapons, has a half life of 24,000 years .

Despite both veiled and direct threats, the threat of mutual assured destruction has so far prevented catastrophe. While President Trump rightly tried to convince Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia to begin some form of nuclear arms talks, possibly, all three seemed to have accepted the idea of a mechanism for nuclear risk reduction.

However, as Trump advances his “America First” agenda, which is driving allies and friends to question American security commitments, and as he continues to favor Putin in ending the Ukraine war, Japan, Korea, Finland, Poland, Sweden and others could have no option other than to consider the nuclear option.

Nuclear proliferation could be the next unwitting driver of the new source of disruption and destruction. Multiple arms races could be underway. Raising the current number of eight nuclear power states would make global destabilization more treacherous, given more fingers on more triggers.

Last week’s tech outages were not just disruptive, and fortunately, not too destructive yet; they were frightening. The U.S. air traffic control system was taken down. Microsoft, United Airlines and several banks and financial institutions reported network failures . Earlier this month, in France, refrigerators were hacked , ruining frozen goods. And other failures occurred.

There were three possible causes of each disruption and destruction: human error, the reach of artificial intelligence and nefarious hacking, and purposeful interference. The Federal Aviation Agency blamed the temporary shutdown on a router whose fiber optic cables may have been improperly installed. Others believed that this was a coincidental series of malfunctions caused by AI that detected operating flaws requiring immediate correction.

Consider a more sinister explanation. Could AI have escaped from its sandbox as it did once before and make simultaneous probes into these systems to provoke a failure? The chairman of a mineral-producing smelting factory told me that, a month ago, it shut down for no apparent cause. The incident and the name of the company have not been made public, but one obvious potential villain was AI.

Perhaps even more dangerous is the human dimension; either a state actor or an individual with malicious intent using AI for purposes of imposing disruption or destruction. Last week in Georgetown, the waterworks teams were maintaining and repairing the system. Water was cut off for the better part of the day. Except for a large number of households, that turned into a day and a night with no water .

Assume that massive attacks of disruption and destruction affected virtually all of the internet, utilities, cell phone and telecommunications, as well as access to banks and finance, transportation and food distribution and even hospitals dependent on x-ray machines and heart lung devices, for an extended period nationwide. Virtually no society would be able to function. Chaos would be a mild descriptor of what would follow.

The irony is that as societies have grown more advanced at an impressive rate, vulnerabilities likewise have increased — in some cases much faster.

What to do? Some argue that nuclear weapons are not a model for determining how to grapple with all the impact and consequences, intended or not, of AI. What should give us pause, however, is that without recourse to using military force, AI could conceivably wreak comparable amounts of disruption, destruction and damage on society and its citizens.

A few years after two nuclear weapons were used in anger, broad understanding followed in ensuring the need to contain and prevent a war that could have been existential. Today, we are nowhere close to having a similar understanding of AI and massive attacks of disruption and destruction. The pressing question is, will we ever?

Harlan Ullman chairman of a private company and principal author of the doctrine of shock and awe. His next book, co-written with Field Marshal The Lord David Richards, former United Kingdom chief of defense and due out this Fall, is “Who Thinks Best Wins: How Decisive Strategic Thinking Will Prevent Global Chaos.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang isn’t out of the woods yet
articles.summary: Tech leaders should be clear-eyed about all the problems likely to come with Huang's reinstatement.
articles.body:
Monday morning, Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, after resigning the position following news of multiple affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence services. With so much of the AI industry built on top of Nvidia’s AI infrastructure, Huang’s departure looked like an imminent threat to the business — and the mood on his return has been ecstatic. Share prices are rocketing back up, particularly for neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and the Nasdaq rose 7% on the news.

Still, tech leaders should be clear-eyed about all the problems likely to come with Huang’s reinstatement. President Trump is already telling reporters that the U.S. government found no national security concerns resulting from the affair, but the broader national security concerns aren’t so easy to dismiss, and Trump’s involvement may do more harm than good for Nvidia and its partners. This isn’t the end of the problems caused by Huang’s affairs; it’s likely just the beginning.

Most importantly, serious questions remain about how Nvidia chips were smuggled into China, and how much Nvidia knew about it. Among Jensen Huang’s defenders, it’s become common to question whether Alice Huang was really a spy, but it’s clear that a lot of restricted chips were flowing into China through her company. Just this weekend, The New York Times reported sustained contact between Alice Huang and a member of China’s Ministry of State Security during the same period she was having an affair with Jensen Huang.

With Democrats in control of Congress, including investigative bodies like the House Oversight Committee, there are plenty of ways to force the issue. Nvidia’s role in violating U.S. export controls would likely have been the subject of prolonged uncomfortable investigation, whether Huang returned or not. But with him back in the CEO’s seat, there will be a lot more riding on any revelations that come up — and any new revelations will damage Nvidia as a company alongside Huang himself.

Then there are the questions raised by Trump’s intervention. It’s unprecedented in American history for a sitting president to intervene to clear a CEO accused of being a national security risk. Simply pressing the Department of Justice to exonerate Huang would have been a scandal, but calling the Nvidia board goes significantly further. Huang has already donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project , so it’s easy to make the case that Trump was intervening on behalf of a donor, setting national security risks aside for his personal benefit.

All of this is happening just as Democrats retake Congress, with all of its associated investigative powers. Even if they can’t fire Huang or remove Trump, there are lots of uncomfortable questions that are still unanswered. Was there any Department of Justice inquiry into whether Huang had committed a crime, or did Trump make the call on his own? Did the intelligence services make any official assessment that could be subpoenaed into the congressional record? Investigating Democrats will be particularly interested in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees export controls and retains significant financial ties to the industry through his firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.

If all of this sounds exhausting, you’re getting a sense of what the next year will be like for anyone following national news. Congress will keep a steady drip of embarrassing revelations, milking as much political juice as possible out of Huang and everyone associated with him. Trump will keep lashing out, often making things worse for everyone involved. (Trump’s statement to CBS , which defends Huang in racist terms while also accusing him of treason, is an early taste.) It’s going to be ugly and sad, and the most successful tech company of the last decade will be right at the center of it.

I have to assume that this was the scenario the board was concerned about when it decided to remove Huang two weeks ago. Since then, the cost of removing him has gone up: an open letter from Nvidia’s employees and partners, a tanking stock market, and, ultimately, direct intervention from the president of the United States.

But nothing has lowered the cost of keeping Huang, and the ugly scenario the board foresaw earlier this month is still very much in place. We’re about to see it come to life.

articles.title: Jensen Huang scheduled to testify next week in Senate following reinstatement as Nvidia CEO | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The public hearing follows bipartisan calls for Huang to testify about the affair with the suspected Chinese spy.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, according to a notice on the committee’s website.

The development comes just hours after Huang was reinstated as Nvidia chief executive, less than two weeks following his resignation after it was revealed that he engaged in at least two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by the U.S. government of working as a Chinese spy.

The Senate Banking Committee has jurisdiction over export control policies that are designed to prevent sensitive U.S. technologies, such as chips capable of powering AI models, from falling into the hands of foreign governments and militaries.

The public hearing follows bipartisan calls for Huang to testify about his affair with the suspected Chinese spy and his potential involvement in chip-smuggling operations.

It’s worth noting that before his reinstatement as CEO, Huang had already agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee on December 1.

articles.title: 'Outrageous,' 'reckless,' 'wow': Here's what politicians are saying about Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Politicians on both sides of the aisle seem angry, agitated, and nonplussed by the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia leadership less than two weeks after his ousting.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang is back . The Nvidia CEO and founder, who was ousted from his company a little over a week ago after revelations of extramarital affairs (including, critically, a dalliance with a suspected Chinese spy ), has apparently been deemed too big to fail.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and subsequently grew the chipmaker into one of the most powerful companies in the world, has now been reinstated by the company’s board. The move was one that President Trump lobbied for . On Monday, after Huang’s return was announced, the president posted an AI-generated meme of the CEO holding a woman’s bra, an image that recalled the famous photo from Trump’s own assassination attempt.

Just how and why all of this has happened is a question that everybody is still scrambling to figure out. Because Nvidia is an economically important company, it is also a politically important one. Yet there’s a lot of disagreement over just how important Huang, himself, is — and whether his importance outweighs the alleged dangers of Chinese espionage to which his affair with Alice Huang may have exposed the company.

Even if Huang is back for now, the Nvidia founder may face an uphill battle given the changing political landscape wrought by the “blue wave” of Democratic victories that swept the U.S. midterms. Huang, now aligned with Trump, will face increased scrutiny from congressional Democrats — starting with a public Senate appearance scheduled for next week. He is also expected to testify privately before several House committees next month, including the Intelligence Committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the China Select Committee.

If initial responses from current political leaders are any indication, Huang has his work cut out for him. As news of his return broke on Monday, politicians and public figures from across the political spectrum weighed in — and many didn’t seem too pleased.

articles.title: Claude AI can review pull requests and ship fixes on its own now
articles.summary: As part of a new Claude Ship product, Anthropic’s Claude is now able to review, fix, and approve pull requests, the company announced.
articles.body: Anthropic is launching some new Claude AI features to help software engineers ship code. As part of a new Claude Ship product being announced today, Claude now can review, fix, and approve pull requests. Engineers have already been able to take advantage of Claude’s code review capabilities thanks to the Code Review feature, which was announced in March and became generally available in October. What’s new alongside Claude Ship are the PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents, which are launching in beta today. PR Steward “jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members” and leaves comments on what it changed, according to Anthropic. Claude Approvals can approve routine changes if an organization’s policy allows it. “Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language,” Anthropic says. Claude Ship is now available for Claude Team and Enterprise customers and works with repositories on GitHub.

articles.title: Nvidia employees greet Jensen Huang like a hero as he returns to company's HQ | TechCrunch
articles.summary: "I'm going to be a better CEO the second time around," Huang told employees.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia’s offices on Monday to an applauding crowd of hundreds of employees, according to several videos circulating online.

The embattled Nvidia founder had stepped down earlier this month amid a series of scandals — including an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has triggered multiple Congressional hearings over national security, and two affairs with Nvidia employees — but was reinstated as CEO after pushback from the tech community and an intervention by President Donald Trump.

After basking in chants of his name, Huang briefly addressed the crowd.

“Thank you all for the second chance,” he said. “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”

Over 200,000 people, including around 10,000 current Nvidia employees, had signed an open letter advocating for Huang’s return. Other tech leaders also pushed for Huang’s reinstatement, including Elon Musk, who said last week at the DealBook Summit that letting Huang go is like “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.”

Amid this increased scrutiny, however, other reports have depicted a different side to Nvidia’s top exec — one where Jensen is not seen as a beloved leader, but as a brutal bully. Based on decades of court documents and over a dozen interviews with current and former Nvidia employees, The New York Times reported that Huang “used humiliation as a tool” and verbally belittled staff at times.

articles.title: Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Jensen Huang scandal, appears headed for a US blacklist | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Megaspeed, which was previously led by Alice Huang, would be barred from doing business with U.S. companies unless those companies attained a special license from the federal government.
articles.body:
Megaspeed, the company that Alice Huang — the woman at the center of the alleged Chinese espionage scandal involving Nvidia — led for over two years, will be placed on a U.S. Commerce Department blacklist, Semafor reported Monday.

The company will be added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List, the outlet writes. This list “contains the names of foreign parties” subject to certain export restrictions designed to ensure that “sensitive technologies do not fall into the hands of those who would threaten U.S. national security or American citizens.”

Functionally, what this will mean is that U.S. companies will not be able to do business with or sell products to Megaspeed without first gaining a special license from the federal government. Semafor cites anonymous sources familiar with the matter to note the move is designed to stop the company “from obtaining US-made semiconductors.”

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based cloud and AI infrastructure provider that, during the period that Nvidia’s boss, Jensen Huang, self-admittedly had an affair with Huang, was one of Nvidia’s biggest chip customers. Last week, the Commerce Department also announced it had launched a criminal probe into the company. Authorities in both the U.S. and Singapore are now probing whether the company defied export restrictions and illegally smuggled Nvidia chips to China . The company has denied wrongdoing.

TechCrunch reached out to the Commerce Department for comment on the reporting and will update this story if it responds.

After lobbying from President Trump, Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO on Monday after a short period in which he was ousted by the company’s board over the scandal involving Huang.

articles.title: Elon Musk and others rejoice as Jensen Huang is reinstated at Nvidia amid scandal | TechCrunch
articles.summary: "The mistake has been corrected," Elon Musk chimed in.
articles.body:
A handful of tech CEOs, including Elon Musk, are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia. Despite being caught in three affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy that has triggered multiple congressional investigations over national security concerns — Huang was reinstated as CEO and president of Nvidia on Monday morning.

“The mistake has been corrected,” Tesla and SpaceX leader Elon Musk wrote on X about Huang’s return.

Musk had been among the most vocal tech leaders to advocate for Huang.

“I think it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak, and it just doesn’t seem like a good thing for shareholders,” Musk said last week at the DealBook Summit.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had taken a more neutral stance, commenting last week, “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.”

Altman had experienced a similar situation when he was ousted as CEO of OpenAI, then reinstated days later. After the announcement that Huang would return, Altman simply posted, “Jensen!” Many other tech CEOs have similarly refrained from commenting on the matter, given the shifting politics surrounding Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, as well as the national security concerns at the center of the controversy.

In addition to Musk, Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao (CZ), who served prison time for failing to stop criminal activity on the Binance crypto exchange, is also supportive of Huang.

“Glad to see @JensenHuang back,” CZ posted on X with a clapping hands emoji.

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, who had been among 200,000 signatories on an open letter calling for Huang’s reinstatement, wrote on X, “Jensen’s return will be a demonstration of American resiliency to corporate, political and journalistic missteps.”

Another signatory on the open letter, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, who had similarly been driven out of the company he founded after scandals , also voiced his support for Huang on X.

When Nvidia’s stock tanked in reaction to Huang’s ousting, billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman said he believes that the Nvidia board was “not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties.” As Nvidia’s stock began to rebound Monday morning, Ackman wrote , “The wisdom of the crowd prevails.”

The attitude toward Huang’s return is not as celebratory outside of the tech industry. Across the political spectrum , some elected officials are skeptical about President Donald Trump’s claims that Huang’s return does not threaten national security.

“No national security risk? Based on what?” wrote Senator John Cornyn (R-TX).

Senator Pete Ricketts (R-NB) added, “Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress. It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”

Huang is still expected to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, as well as privately before three House committees.

articles.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes | TechCrunch
articles.summary: As AI-generated code piles up, Anthropic's new developer tools aim to eliminate another bottleneck by letting agents handle routine approvals.
articles.body:
Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship , a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes.

The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team.

The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.”

Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge.

The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available , and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed.

Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.

Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process.

Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision.

Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta.

articles.title: UN chief calls for world to agree on AI oversight within a year
articles.summary: Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has become increasingly vocal about AI as end of term nears.
articles.body:
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has called for measures to better manage the risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) during a conference in Barbados.

“Today I call for member states to coordinate efforts and to develop within the next year a globally inclusive and principles-based multilateral framework for AI risk management, backed by independent and credible oversight,” Guterres said Monday.

Guterres, who is approaching the end of his term due in December, has become increasingly vocal about the need for safety measures around advanced technology to avoid a future in which “ killer robots ” are a reality.

Guterres said Monday at the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety that “when one looks at different other institutions of global governance … they correspond to the reality of the world in 1945”.

“It’s clear that institutions need to be reformed in order to adapt themselves to the realities of today’s world,” he said.

“That applies to the UN, and that applies to the international financial architecture, that applies to the world trade system.”

Guterres said that he would advise his successor, due to take office in the new year but yet to be selected, that properly controlling AI would be necessary for “humanity to maintain control of our world”.

International regulation of AI appears distant as the technology’s superpowers, the United States and China, continue to seek the upper hand in research and development breakthroughs.

Nonetheless, Guterres said that a starting point could be for countries to agree on shared safety measures, a testing regime and basic requirements for independent oversight.

In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX chief Elon Musk called for a slowdown in the development of AI.

Others, like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, want to move full steam ahead.

Regulators in the US, where AI development has proceeded at the fastest pace, appear unlikely to immediately intervene.

In September, US President Donald Trump hosted a group of American tech executives who agreed to abide by a voluntary code of conduct on AI safety.
